id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12808v2
published: 2021-07-27T13:30:07Z
summary: In this work we create agents that can perform well beyond a single, individual task, that exhibit much wider generalisation of behaviour to a massive, rich space of challenges. We define a universe of tasks within an environment domain and demonstrate the ability to train agents that are generally capable across this vast space and beyond. The environment is natively multi-agent, spanning the continuum of competitive, cooperative, and independent games, which are situated within procedurally generated physical 3D worlds. The resulting space is exceptionally diverse in terms of the challenges posed to agents, and as such, even measuring the learning progress of an agent is an open research problem. We propose an iterative notion of improvement between successive generations of agents, rather than seeking to maximise a singular objective, allowing us to quantify progress despite tasks being incomparable in terms of achievable rewards. We show that through constructing an open-ended learning process, which dynamically changes the training task distributions and training objectives such that the agent never stops learning, we achieve consistent learning of new behaviours. The resulting agent is able to score reward in every one of our humanly solvable evaluation levels, with behaviour generalising to many held-out points in the universe of tasks. Examples of this zero-shot generalisation include good performance on Hide and Seek, Capture the Flag, and Tag. Through analysis and hand-authored probe tasks we characterise the behaviour of our agent, and find interesting emergent heuristic behaviours such as trial-and-error experimentation, simple tool use, option switching, and cooperation. Finally, we demonstrate that the general capabilities of this agent could unlock larger scale transfer of behaviour through cheap finetuning.

title: The Inclusion Depth of Pattern Languages: An Open Problem in Algorithmic Learning Theory
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30389v1
published: 2026-05-28T11:19:25Z
summary: Pattern languages are a classical model in formal language theory and algorithmic learning theory. This note formulates the problem of computing the inclusion depth of a pattern language: the length of the longest strict inclusion chain from the universal pattern language to the language generated by a given pattern. Inclusion depth captures the mind-change complexity of pattern identification from positive data. The central open question is whether the inclusion depth ID_Sigma(p) is computable for every pattern p over every finite alphabet Sigma with at least two symbols, and whether it is computable in polynomial time. A simple conjectured formula, ID_Sigma(p) = 2|p| - #var(p) - 1, would imply a linear-time algorithm. The problem connects pattern language inclusion, combinatorics on words, language identification in the limit, and mind-change-bounded learning.

title: IPPOG : Bridging the gap between science education at school and modern scientific research
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2011.14743v1
published: 2020-11-30T12:56:40Z
summary: The International Particle Physics Outreach Group (IPPOG) has been making concerted and systematic efforts to present and popularise particle physics across all audiences and age groups since 1997. Today the scientific community has in IPPOG a strategic pillar in fostering long-term, sustainable support for fundamental research around the world. One of the main tools IPPOG has been offering to the scientific community, teachers and educators for almost 10 years is the Resource Database (RDB), an online platform containing a collection of high quality engaging education and outreach materials in particle physics and related sciences.

article.body:
Think of an automated thermostat in a smart building that must follow strict energy-saving rules while deciding on its own when to cool a room during an unexpected heatwave. Our computer workers examined how systems divide their internal resources between planning strategies and executing actions to handle such dual pressures. Paper-supported readings suggest that systems work best when they partition, which means separate, these heavy reasoning tasks instead of trying to do everything at once. [1]

The teams recorded how these systems encounter reasoning blind spots during complex language and logic tasks. Paper-supported findings indicate that failure attribution, which means tracking down the exact step where an error occurred, helps models spot their own mistakes. However, some planned work faced temporary deferrals due to provider tool delays while the teams were attempting to run their analyses. [2]

Researchers also looked at physical frameworks and found that traditional scientific theories struggle to model adaptive agents in changing environments. When examining high-stakes scenarios, paper-supported readings show that strict obedience to rules can become a failure of intelligence if safety-critical constraints are ignored. In parallel work, teams explored how cultural transmission and past experiences help shape behavioral preferences. [3, 4, 5]

When humans rely too heavily on automated recommendations, studies suggest it can lead to reduced self-regulation and increased hesitation. To address this, other teams integrated preference oracle frameworks, which means generalized systems for evaluating agent alignment without fixed reward functions. Episodic memory recall was also studied as a way to provide stability by helping systems remember past choices. [6, 7, 8]

Workers mapped out curiosity-driven learning where systems use arousal mechanisms to explore information and form unassigned goals. Using multi-objective optimization methods, systems learned to prioritize different policies dynamically. While some communication frameworks help align multi-agent values, preference stability ultimately relies on how well models resolve conflicts between internal rules and external stimuli. [9, 10, 11, 12]

Summary

Our groups studied how autonomous computer systems balance planning, following rules, and adapting to new information. We reviewed papers on error tracking, memory, and goal setting, while noting some temporary delays in our scheduled research. We are still trying to understand how these systems can safely set their own goals without needing constant human supervision.
article.lede: Our computer workers are investigating how independent systems balance strict instructions with the need to adapt when situations change unexpectedly.
article.lens: We examine these computer models by looking at how they balance external rules with self-guided learning, much like a person deciding whether to follow a recipe or adapt when ingredients run out.
article.title: Tracing How Intelligent Systems Handle Unexpected Choices and Rules

compacts.rule: Computational creativity frameworks require robust integration between formulation and evaluation components, supported by active inference and drift-diffusion mechanisms, for agents to autonomously navigate and identify novel, worthwhile problems.

limitations: Compacts are deterministic receipt annotations, not authoritative durable state.
They do not enter provider context in shadow mode.
A compact never deletes, replaces, or proves its underlying evidence.
trust_compacts_shadow.principle: Compress settled operational consequences without severing their evidence roots.

recent_notebooks.summary: Agent continuity is instrumentally valuable as a mechanism for sustaining problem formulation and evaluation in non-stationary environments. Active inference frameworks suggest that persistence (continuity) is required to resolve conflicts between internal policy models and external stimuli (cognitive effort).
